Board: all six panels

Here is the SO-101 arm drawing a kitten on a Wacom tablet. By the end of part 6, the pen was missing its target by about a millimeter. That was with the best correction held fixed during drawing: 1.057 mm RMS on the real arm, over the drawings I use to choose controllers. RMS means you square every distance error, average the squares and take the square root, so a few large misses weigh more than many small ones.

So where does that last millimeter come from, and what removes it? I have four tools. I can learn a correction from practice, between drawings. I can read the joint encoders during a stroke and react. I can bypass the servo's own position loop and drive the motor myself. And I can build a simulated arm, a digital twin, and try ideas there first. Meanwhile the hardware keeps changing under me: friction shifts, motors warm up, nibs get swapped. Each tool attacks a different kind of miss, and you can only tell which by splitting the error the right way. Let's split it.

Every result below carries a tag. Measured: the real arm ran, and each result says whether it scores joint tracking or pen error on the tablet. Offline: I analyzed recordings the arm already made. Simulation: the twin drew. Dry run: only the software path ran, which says nothing about precision. Only Measured comparisons rank controllers. The claim check lists the source file, version, metric and cohort behind each number, and figure-data.json holds the frozen plot values.

Subtract two repeats and the bias cancels

Start with the simplest experiment there is. Have the arm draw one practice scribble twice, with the same motion and the same settings. The two pen traces don't land on top of each other. Subtract one from the other, sample by sample: across 96 such pairs, the difference is 0.95 mm RMS (Offline). If each run wobbles independently by about the same amount, the difference of two runs is √2 times one run's wobble, so a single run wobbles by about 0.95 / √2 ≈ 0.67 mm. A separate analysis agrees: in 50 repetitions of one scribble, each run sits 0.72 mm RMS from the average of all 50. So both analyses put the wobble near 0.7 mm. These are two estimates from different recordings, not the endpoints of a confidence interval.

Now look at what the subtraction threw away. Suppose the arm draws some curve a bit low every single time. That shared miss is in both traces, so it cancels in run A minus run B. Repeat spread tells you how repeatable the arm is, and nothing about how close it gets to the target. Panel 1 splits the miss into its two parts:

  • Bias is the part that comes back every run. Because it repeats, you can learn it from practice and subtract it from the next command.
  • Wobble is the part that is new each run. A fixed correction can't know it in advance, so you have to watch the run while it happens.

The 0.7 mm belongs to these drawings, poses, servo gains and nibs. Change them and it can move.

The learned correction fixed the timing

The between-run side looks a lot like supervised learning. The arm draws practice scribbles, and each recording keeps the path I asked for, the joint angles and the path the tablet saw. A model learns which way the pen drifts and pushes the command the other way. Then I freeze it and test it. Each set of drawings has exactly one job:

  • Practice scribbles: the only data the correction is fitted on.
  • Test drawings (a kitten, a star, a spiral and a square): used to choose between controllers, never for fitting.
  • Validation drawings: kept out of fitting and choosing, to check that the choice generalizes.

A first try put a small frozen neural network on top of the part 6 correction. On the real arm, this first network reduced the pen's RMS error on the Test drawings compared with the part 6 correction (Measured). For a later version of this extra network (the correction head), I made the comparison stricter. It trained on N64, a set of 64 practice motions, for 102 passes. On the real arm it got one bracketed block over the four Test drawings: physics baseline, then the head, then the baseline again. The head is compared with the mean of the two baselines around it.

With the usual fixed-time score, the baseline sits at 2.238 mm and the head at 1.643 mm. That's 0.6 mm gone! (This block differs from part 6's, so compare these numbers only with each other.) But a fixed-time score compares the pen with where it should be at the same instant. Picture a pen that draws a perfect kitten slightly late: it gets charged for every millimeter it trails behind. So I scored the same runs again with a lag-adjusted score. It uses the tablet's own report times, fits one constant lag, slides the trace by that lag and keeps every spatial offset, with no rotation or shift to line the shapes up. Lag-adjusted, the baseline sits at 1.537 mm and the head at 1.641 mm.

Same runs, two metrics, opposite rankings (panel 2). Inside that block, the evidence supports a timing improvement and does not support a better shape. With a drifting baseline, unequal training-pass counts and one block per head, it also can't tell you how heads scale with more data.

Full plot: timing-and-shape.svg.

A frozen head also answers a smaller question than the one I care about. The plan is continual learning: keep collecting practice and keep updating, so the correction follows slow drift as friction, temperature and the nib change. The score that counts is the error the arm sustains over a long deployment, and one early low point says little about that. To measure it, I need to compare controllers over long runs while giving them the same number of practice passes. That experiment isn't finished.

Encoder prediction weakens as the delay grows

The learned correction takes care of what repeats. What about the 0.7 mm that doesn't? Each joint has an encoder that reports its angle throughout the stroke, so first: can the encoders even see the wobble? I took 40 repetitions of practice scribble s40, all with the old nib, the physics controller phys and fixed servo gains P16, and subtracted the mean path from each run. What's left is 0.69 mm RMS of pure wobble (Offline).

Joint angles read at the same instant explain about 70% of its variance, and the wrist-flex joint contributes the most. My earlier explainer said most of this variation was invisible to the encoders. That was wrong. These are shares of squared deviation, so 70% and 30% don't split 0.69 mm into two distances.

Now the catch. A controller can't use the reading from the same instant, because between reading an angle and the motor responding, the pen has moved on. Feedback has to predict the deviation early enough to act on it, using only readings that have already arrived. So I asked the recordings a stricter question: from encoder history alone, how much of the deviation can you predict a given delay ahead? At 50 ms, 48%. At 100 ms, 27%. At 150 ms, 11%. At 200 ms, 5%.

Turn the 100 ms point into millimeters. In a stroke-only analysis (a separate cut from the 0.69 mm figure), explaining 27% of the variance leaves 73%, and √0.73 ≈ 0.85, so 0.71 mm becomes 0.61 mm. A quarter of the variance buys a tenth of a millimeter. That is a best case predicted from recordings. No closed loop has removed that error yet, and the analysis leaves out how new feedback would interact with the existing controller.

You need enough encoder history to make a useful prediction, and the motor has to act before that prediction goes stale. Actuator delay pushes the prediction further ahead, exactly where the signal fades. Remember that we subtracted the average path of these old-nib runs, so all of this measures how far each run wanders from that average and leaves out any miss they all share.

Full plot: repeat-budget.svg.

Direct drive runs into breakaway friction

Some of that delay and hidden behavior lives inside the servo. Normally I send it a position goal, and its internal loop decides how to get there, with friction, delay and its own motion behavior tucked inside. Direct drive moves the boundary. My loop reads the encoder and chooses the motor duty, the fraction of time the motor is powered, for the base-pan joint.

On 13 Oct, with duty capped at 12%, the pan joint tracked its reference to 1.68 mrad RMS (Measured). This score lines each encoder reading up with the reference at the time of the reading, a correction to an earlier explainer that used the reference at the command's aim time. At a 20% cap it got worse, 3.91 mrad: the joint fell into a steady oscillation (a limit cycle), and more steady duty didn't fix it in that test. On 14 Oct, at the same 12% cap, two runs gave 3.08 and 10.40 mrad. The joint now needed more drive just to start moving.

That's breakaway friction, and it changed overnight. The control problem it poses is clear: push hard enough to unstick the joint, then back off before it overshoots. These are joint angles, though, not pen-tip distances, and there is no completed tablet comparison against the current controller. Until there is, direct drive can't be ranked on pen precision.

A twin has to miss where the arm misses

Every experiment so far costs time on a real arm that keeps changing. A digital twin would let me test in software. Mine simulates the controller and joints, then works out where the pen would land on a virtual tablet. It includes friction, contact and the flex that makes the pen trail behind. An optional learned add-on tries to cover what the physics misses. When is it good enough? Matching the arm's overall RMS is too weak a test, because two traces can miss by the same RMS in completely different places. The twin has to miss at the same samples, in the same direction.

So the score is the share of the real arm's squared pen error that the twin reproduces, sample by sample. 100% is perfect agreement. 0% is what you get by predicting no error at all. Below zero is worse than that.

The best variant, c2 + play, adds a fitted term shaped like mechanical play. On the original 72 passes, it reproduces 49.6% of the arm's squared error. Those are also recordings I used during development, so this is the easier test. With the traces aligned as in the study, the arm and twin differ by 1.30 mm RMS. On a held-out date, 13 Oct, with 28 passes, it scores −5.6%, with a mismatch of 1.25 mm. Both compare Simulation with Offline logs. The absolute mismatch barely moved. The real arm moved: with a changed nib, setup and controller mix it erred less, so the same-size mismatch became a bigger share of its error. Either way, the twin failed to transfer across dates (panel 5).

The play term was fitted, so it doesn't identify a real gear gap. Geometry, contact and breakaway friction need to be pulled apart with independent data before the twin can rank real controllers. Spring-scale and pen tests come next, to measure lateral stiffness and drag and give the contact model physical limits. An IMU set is ordered too: its accelerometer could catch shaking and bending that a rigid-joint model misses, once a tablet comparison shows it helps.

Full plot: twin-across-days.svg.

Learned correction plus encoder feedback, with delay as the weak spot

Panel 6 puts the four tools side by side. I'd combine two of them: learn the miss that comes back every run, then use encoder readings as they arrive to catch this run's wobble. That's the direction I favor, and the next experiments come straight from the gaps above:

  1. Characterize breakaway, then run a fair direct-drive drawing comparison on the tablet.
  2. Test drive scheduling and mechanical friction changes as separate candidates.
  3. Build an external-camera station with known touch points that recalibrates geometry and tool position from time to time. It won't measure stroke error continuously.

General 3D motion, varying payloads, IMU correction in operation and a calibrated station are all still untested.

If you have a precision task of your own, the method carries over. Subtract two repeats to see how much the miss changes between runs, and compare their average with the target to find the miss they share. Send the shared part to a learned correction and the fresh part to feedback, check your delay budget before you count on feedback, and score with a metric that can't be won by fixing timing alone.

The head lowers fixed-time RMS from 2.238 to 1.643 mm. What must you check before you conclude that the drawing improved?

Answer. Score the same runs lag-adjusted against the bracketing baseline. Here the baseline drops to 1.537 mm and the head sits at 1.641 mm, so the gain was timing and the shape did not get better. Then confirm that the head was chosen on Test drawings, checked on validation drawings and never scored on its own practice data, and that the comparison is Measured.

The arithmetic behind √2 and the lag adjustment

Write run A as target + bias + wobbleA and run B as target + bias + wobbleB. Then A − B = wobbleA − wobbleB, and the target and the bias are gone. If the two wobbles are independent with the same RMS σ, their variances add, so RMS(A − B) = √2 σ. With 0.95 mm, σ ≈ 0.67 mm. Accuracy is the distance from the target, which keeps the bias, so the two numbers measure different things.

The fixed-time error at time t is pen(t) − target(t). The lag-adjusted error is pen(t + τ) − target(t), with one constant lag τ fitted from the tablet's native report times. Only τ is fitted. Nothing rotates or shifts the trace, so any spatial bias stays in the score.
